title.en: The torch that would not glow

text.en:
Meena's torch did not light. She opened it and found the battery had slipped so that it did not touch the metal strip.
She pushed it back and the bulb glowed.
"The path was broken," she said.

An electric circuit is a closed path along which electric current flows. A simple circuit has a cell or battery, a bulb, wires and a switch.
When the switch is on (closed), current flows from the cell through the wires and bulb and back, so the bulb glows. When the switch is off (open) the path is broken and the bulb does not glow.
Conductors such as metals let current pass. Insulators such as rubber, plastic and wood do not. Never touch mains electricity or play with sockets. Use only cells for experiments.
An electric circuit is a closed path for current. It has a cell, a bulb, wires and a switch.
When the switch is closed, current flows and the bulb glows.
When the switch is open, the path is broken and the bulb does not glow.
Metals conduct. Rubber and plastic do not. Never touch mains electricity.

problem.en: A bulb in a circuit does not glow. Give two things to check.

text.en: Check whether the switch is closed.

why.en: An open switch breaks the path.

text.en: Check the wires, the cell and the bulb connections.

why.en: A loose wire breaks the path too.

text.en: A closed, complete path makes the bulb glow.

why.en: Also check that the bulb is not fused.

prompt.en: A friend says a bulb will glow with just one wire to the cell. How will you explain?

requiredIdeas.en: Current needs a complete closed path.
One wire does not make a loop.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking electricity needs only one connection.

points.en: A circuit is a closed path with a cell, wires, a bulb and a switch.
The bulb glows only when the circuit is closed.
Metals conduct; rubber and plastic insulate.
